title: Cystoid Macular Edema (CME): The Clinician’s Masterclass
summary: Cystoid Macular Edema (CME) represents the final common pathway for diverse retinal pathologies, characterized by fluid accumulation in the Henle layer. Mastering its diagnosis and multi-modal treatment is fundamental to preserving central visual acuity in the clinical setting.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: CME is a distinct retinal condition characterized by fluid accumulation within the outer plexiform layer (Henle's layer). Pathophysiologically, it results from the breakdown of the Inner Blood-Retinal Barrier (iBRB) at the level of the retinal vascular endothelium or the Outer Blood-Retinal Barrier (oBRB) at the RPE. This leads to increased permeability, secondary to inflammatory mediators (Prostaglandins, VEGF, IL-6), surgical trauma, or venous stasis.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Hierarchy
content: Step 1: Dilated Fundus Exam: Evaluate for foveal thickening and loss of foveal reflex.
Step 2: SD-OCT: Gold standard to quantify Central Subfield Thickness (CST) and map intraretinal cystic spaces.
Step 3: Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): Demonstrates late-phase 'petaloid' hyperfluorescence.
Step 4: Ancillary: Indocyanine Green (ICG) angiography for occult choroidal pathology if suspecting inflammatory etiology.

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: First-line: Topical NSAIDs (e.g., Nepafenac 0.1%, Bromfenac 0.09%) for 4-8 weeks.
Second-line: Intravitreal Anti-VEGF (Ranibizumab, Aflibercept) for chronic cases.
Third-line: Intravitreal Steroids (Dexamethasone implant, Triamcinolone) for uveitic CME.
Surgical: Pars Plana Vitrectomy if vitreous traction or residual membrane is present.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Refer/Escalate
content: Acute pain or signs of endophthalmitis post-op

content.explanation: P: Post-surgical (Irvine-Gass); E: Edema (Diabetic); T: Thrombosis (RVO); A: Autoimmune/Uveitis; L: Latrogenic (Drugs).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always perform a 360-degree scleral depression or fundus exam to rule out peripheral pathology in unexplained CME.
Irvine-Gass syndrome typically presents 4-6 weeks post-cataract surgery.
CST on OCT is more reliable than clinical exam for monitoring treatment response.
Topical steroids and NSAIDs exhibit synergy; consider combination therapy for refractory cases.
